html:
"Celtic kingdoms" is the map's label for small kingdoms whose people spoke Celtic languages, at the edges of the British Isles. The label moves. On the maps for 800 and 900 it marks the lands around the Solway and the Clyde, in what is now southern Scotland and Cumbria. On the maps for 1000 to 1200 it covers Ireland.

In the north of Britain this was the realm of the Britons of the Kingdom of Strathclyde, who spoke a language close to Welsh. Their fortress on Dumbarton Rock fell to Vikings in 870, and by the 1000s their lands were absorbed into Scotland, beside the old lands of the Picts.

Ireland was split among many Gaelic kings who competed for the title of high king. Brian Boru came closest to ruling the whole island and died at the Battle of Clontarf in 1014, fought against Leinster and its Norse allies of Dublin. From 1169 the Anglo-Norman invasion brought much of the island under the English crown, while Gaelic kings held on in the west and north.
